items.title: Jimmy Heath interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, September 8, 2014
items.q: But I was with Dizzy’s band when the Orioles had it

ctx.x: No I didn’t see anything that was worrisome because we had different genres, and we still have different genres of music. So I didn’t have a problem with people, quartets singing, Orioles singing songs, “What Are You Doing New Years,” or whatever the song. That

was the one that was popular. But I was with Dizzy’s band when the Orioles had it — they were the headliners. And Dizzy’s band was not. We were on the program with them. So you know, there is still different genres, and what they call R&B, rock & roll, or whatever, they all have some close — they borrowed some things from the jazz idiom too.
Did you ever look upon guys like Sam the Man Taylor and King Curtis and wonder, I wonder if I should try to be getting into that studio business.

items.title: Jimmy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Well I played with a lot of the others like Gil Evans’ Band, Thad Jones’ Band, Dizzy’s Band, of course. Dizzy’s my favorite, he’s my mentor.

ctx.x: Of the giants, who you’ve talked about, are there any giants with whom you did not get to play?

Duke Ellington, Count Basie…Well I played with a lot of the others like Gil Evans’ Band, Thad Jones’ Band, Dizzy’s Band, of course. Dizzy’s my favorite, he’s my mentor. I think of Dizzy Gillespie everyday, like my parents. He flashes through my mind at some time during the day. Miles, not as much, but he was talented. People ask

me all the time, I got an email this morning before I came here. Somebody wants to do something about Coltrane and I said, “I’ve been talking about Coltrane for 40 years now, 43.” He passed when he was 40. Everybody’s talking about, “Well, you were with ‘Trane…” Well, yeah! Copy what’s in the other book! I said it, I’m not going to create anything new about Coltrane cause you want to create another book.
